newsitem.title: FRANCE: French farmers see EU biofuel compromise.
newsitem.headline: French farmers see EU biofuel compromise.

text.p: French farmers said on Wednesday that France and the European Union were moving towards a compromise over French tax breaks for biofuels.
Earlier the European Commission ruled against existing French tax breaks for biofuels, saying they discriminated against other European biofuel products.
But in the same statement the Commission said it might approve the scheme in the future if the exemption system was modified to meet competition and Common Agricultural Policy rules.

French industry sources said the Commission opposed the existing sheme because it provided tax breaks for biofuels derived from crops grown on set-aside land only and applied to domestic raw materials and not to imported biofuels.
The scheme exempts crop-based biofuels from an excise tax on petroleum products.
But they also disclosed that France had agreed to modify the existing system to extend the tax breaks to imported biofuels and to crops grown on all types of farm land.
They said France had been given assurances that its revised scheme would secure approval from Brussels.
Farmers, who see biofuels as a promising outlet for their wheat, rapeseed and sugar beet crops, had been particularly eager to see the whole tax exemption dispute settled.
"We are satisfied. It looks like the whole issue is being settled," said Alain Jeanroy, director general of the CGB sugar beet planters federation.
In November the French parliament approved a draft law on clean air that made the use of oxygenated components in fuel mandatory by 2000.
But French farmers have said the law would be useless if biofuels lost their tax incentives.
They argue that crop-derived biofuels needed tax breaks to compete against cheaper rival additives like petroleum based Methyl Tertiary Butyl Ether (MTBE).
"The whole experiment is just starting up. It needs incentives to develop," said an official from the AGPB grain growers association.
In June the International Energy Agency (IEA) said France should abandon its costly support for biofuel production from farm crops, limiting its involvement to long-term research.
The IEA said the cost of supporting the programme through tax exemptions could reach two billion francs by the end of the century.
